subject: lonely retirees
one_liner: Async video messages for people with a lot to say and nobody currently on the line. Every message gets watched. We employ a man for this.
brand_voice_notes: Pitched like a B2B async-video tool with enterprise read receipts, sold to retirees who record 50-minute updates about the gutters. The joke is the analytics: view-duration graphs, drop-off at 0:04, and Craig, a salaried staff viewer who guarantees every message is watched by at least one human. Never pity the users. They are power users. The product treats them like a sales team.

hero.sub: Natter records your video message, uploads it overnight and tells you the moment somebody watched any of it. Usually that somebody is Craig. Craig is very attentive.

features.title: Guaranteed viewership
features.blurb: Every Natter is watched by at least one human, start to finish. If your family doesn't get to it, Craig does. Craig is salaried, has logged 41,000 hours of footage and has opinions about your gutters.

features.title: Forehead-first framing
features.blurb: Our model detects when most of the frame is forehead and labels it Portrait Mode. Recordings made upside down are tagged Artistic. Recordings of the ceiling fan are tagged Ambient. Nothing is ever deleted.

features.title: Automatic chapters
features.blurb: A 53-minute message is split into chapters for the viewer's convenience: Hello, The weather, Your cousin Dale, The weather (cont.), Is this on. Recipients can skip to the end, which is also Is this on.

testimonials.quote: I sent my son 211 messages last year. Craig watched every one and gave a thumbs-up on the one about the furnace. That's more than I got out of the furnace man.
testimonials.name: Harold Benke
testimonials.title: Retired Elevator Inspector, Toledo. Three grandchildren, all on mute.

testimonials.quote: The chapters told me I said 'anyway' 340 times in one video. I've got it down to 290. I'm aiming for the low 200s by spring.

testimonials.quote: My granddaughter says she watches them at double speed. Natter says she watched for four seconds. We both feel heard.

demo_screen_concept: The Natter Library: a video-message dashboard styled like a shelf of rental tapes. A grid of tape cards, each with a thumbnail, a handwritten-style tape label title ('Gutters, part 3'), runtime in VCR on-screen digits (52:14), the recipient, and a viewer status chip: 'Watched by Craig (Staff) 100%', 'Kyle watched 0:04', 'Unopened, 19 days'. Filter tabs by recipient, a fake search, and a sort. Clicking a tape opens a player modal with a scrubbable progress bar, auto-generated chapter list and a viewer-retention graph that falls off a cliff at 0:04 and is held up by Craig alone. Each unwatched tape has a Nudge button whose message escalates on each press ('Did you get my video?' to 'I can see you haven't opened it, Kyle.'). A big REC button opens a recording modal with a blinking REC indicator, a running timecode and a 'forehead coverage' meter that engages Portrait Mode past 70 percent.

design_direction.style: VHS rental-sleeve retro with a VCR on-screen-display layer, living-room daylight mode. The page is staged as a video rental shelf crossed with the blue on-screen menu of a 1994 VCR: tape-label stickers, chunky slab italic titles, the PLAY and REC overlay glyphs, timecode counters and tracking lines. One light mode only. Explicitly absent, because the last seven entries used them: 24-hour sleep bars, Swiss grids, giant numerals, candlelight, foil rules, menu leaders, ruled worksheets, reward stickers, red pen, highlighter swipes, large-print sliders, glossy 8x10s, staples, applause signs, SMPTE bars, pegboard, aisle signs, shelf tags, cork, pins, tape strips. Also absent: dark mode, glassmorphism, blur, neon glow, gradients behind body text. Four motifs carry the page. (1) The tape label: section headers and card titles sit on a white #FFFDF6 sticker with a 1px ink edge, slight -1deg rotation and a printed rule line underneath, like a label someone wrote on in pen. (2) The OSD: VCR on-screen text in VT323, set in white on VCR blue #2340C8 blocks with a hard 2px ink shadow: PLAY, REC, SP, CH 03, timecodes. (3) The tracking line: section dividers are a 14px band of three thin horizontal lines in blue, red and ink, offset a few pixels like a mistracked tape. (4) The REC dot: #D7372A is rationed to the REC dot, the primary CTA and the highlighted tier. Cards are the shape of a VHS spine: wide, short, ink-edged, 3px radius, a hard 4px 4px 0 ink shadow. Headings are Bowlby One, sentence case, slightly italicised via a -6deg skew on the hero only. Body is Karla 17px/1.62. Every timecode, price and count is VT323.
design_direction.archetype: Video-first hero for an async-video SaaS: hero with a CRT-framed 'now playing' tape, feature row, testimonial tapes, three-tier pricing, final CTA.
design_direction.motion_vocab: Hard, instant VCR transitions. The REC dot blinks at 1Hz. The hero timecode counts up in real time. On hover, cards jump 2px up-left and their shadow grows, like a tape pulled half off the shelf. A single tracking-line jitter runs across the hero every few seconds. All of it stops under prefers-reduced-motion.
design_direction.hero_composition_notes: Two columns on desktop. Left: an OSD chip ('PLAY ▶ SP'), the h1 in Bowlby One at clamp(3rem, 7vw, 6.4rem), the sub in Karla, and a REC-red CTA with a blinking dot plus a ghost 'open the demo' button. Right: a chunky beige CRT bezel with rounded glass holding the hero photo of a retiree leaning far too close to a webcam, overlaid with OSD text (REC, a live timecode, 'CH 03') and a faint scanline texture. A tape-label sticker underneath the CRT reads 'Gutters, part 3. DO NOT RECORD OVER'. Stacks to a single column under 860px.

images.rationale: Video-first hero earns a photo (retiree too close to the webcam, framed in a CSS CRT) and doubles as a tape thumbnail in the demo; the demo is a video library, which is photo-shaped, so two tape thumbnails; one testimonial headshot for Harold Benke, the other two testimonials keep their CSS tape-label initials.
